content: Designing a DNA-Based âSmart Photoresistâ Procedure for Electronics Self-Assembly | EECS at UC Berkeley Designing a DNA-Based âSmart Photoresistâ Procedure for Electronics Self-Assembly Erina Iwasa EECS Department, University of California, Berkeley Technical Report No. UCB/ December 1, 2025 Microelectromechanical systems and nanoscale devices are revolutionizing technology, with multifunctional systems unlocking unprecedented possibilities in fields such as biosensors, optics, and energy. These devices integrate diverse components through innovative materials and fabrication processes, culminating in a sophisticated assembly on a unified substrate. Existing top-down serial methods, such as robotic pick and place, are reliable at larger scales but scale down poorly because they face challenges such as alignment error, component fragility, and complexity from increasing amounts of components. To address this, this thesis turns to bottom-up techniques, specifically molecular self-assembly, a powerful approach that offers precise structure control, dynamic adaptability, multifunctionality, and cost-effectiveness. One molecule in particular, DNA, stands out due to its simple but effective programming mechanism (Watson-Crick pairing) to build systems with nanoscale precision. Furthermore, the placement of unique DNA in defined surface locations can enable complex parallel multicomponent assembly. Existing DNA-based methods use standard photoresists to pattern one component at a time or modifications paired with strand displacement. However, these methods require either a repetitive and time-consuming process or multiple modifiers and mechanisms that scale poorly with more complex patterns that are expected in generalizable electronics. This thesis describes the development of an approach that merges existing photoresist processes and DNA to introduce a novel method for multicomponent patterning. We have designed a modified sequence of DNA that integrates photocleavable linkers and surface modifiers to create a âsmart photoresistâ. This âsmart photoresistâ acts as a layer of DNA that is immobilized to substrates before patterning, similar to traditional photoresist. By introducing UV light of a specific wavelength and selectively masking this layer, unique areas of a substrate can be activated for patterning purposes while inactive regions remain available for subsequent steps. A multicomponent-patterned substrate can be produced using a single layer of DNA by repeating this process.
